strengths: Identifies and addresses a highly practical and relevant bottleneck in 3D deep learning: the heavy computational and memory resource costs of reconstructing massive datasets of 3D scenes.
The proposed Micro-Macro decomposition for Tri-Planes is simple, intuitive, and effectively shares global structure across a dataset while keeping scene-specific representations compact.
Demonstrates an impressive reduction in per-scene training time (86%) and storage memory (68%) during the second stage of training, which is highly beneficial when scaling to thousands of scenes.
The manuscript is well-written, with clear figures, an illustrative ablation study, and thorough details in the appendix (including the complete training algorithm and hyperparameters).
weaknesses: The core framework relies heavily on the pre-trained 3D-aware latent space of the IG-AE (Schnepf et al., 2024). The main conceptual novelty is the linear Micro-Macro decomposition on top of it, which is somewhat incremental.

The initial overhead for Stage 1 training is quite high (over 31 hours for 500 scenes). This means the resource benefits only begin to pay off for very large datasets ($N \gg 500$), limiting its utility for small-to-moderate-sized datasets.

The experiments are restricted to highly structured, single-category, well-aligned datasets (ShapeNet Cars and Basel Faces) where global structures are redundant. It is unclear how the method scales to heterogeneous, multi-category, or complex real-world scenes where shared bases might be much harder to learn.

The quantitative evaluation against other fast representation baselines (such as Instant-NGP or TensoRF) is incomplete. While Table 4 compares training times and memory, a comprehensive quality comparison (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) on the same test views is missing, making it hard to evaluate the precise quality-resource trade-offs.

There are some discrepancies in the quantitative results between tables (e.g., Table 1 shows Tri-Planes with 28.56 PSNR on ShapeNet Cars, while Table 4 shows 30.03 PSNR) which are not clearly explained in the text.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and relevant bottleneck in 3D deep learning: the immense computational and memory overhead of fitting implicit/explicit representations (such as NeRFs and Tri-Planes) to large-scale scene datasets.

The proposed Micro-Macro Tri-Plane decomposition is elegant and mathematically straightforward. Splitting features into shared global structures (Macro planes, represented as a linear combination of base planes) and scene-specific details (Micro planes) effectively minimizes the optimization space per scene.
The two-stage training paradigm leverages a 3D-aware latent space, which reduces image resolution and speeds up volume rendering bottlenecks significantly during the second phase.

The experimental evaluation demonstrates massive gains, showing an 86% reduction in per-scene training time and a 68% reduction in memory footprint compared to training standard Tri-Planes independently, with negligible drop in visual quality.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with highly clear figures (e.g., Figure 2) and exhaustive detail in the appendices (including pseudo-code and hyperparameters) ensuring high reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method exhibits a heavy dependency on the first stage (training on $N_1 = 500$ scenes). This warm-up phase requires substantial initial compute ($t_1 = 31.2$ hours), which means the resource-saving benefits only amortize well when the overall dataset is very large ($N \ge 1000$).

Evaluation is limited to relatively simple, well-aligned, and centered datasets (ShapeNet Cars and Basel Faces). It is unclear how well the shared Macro planes (with a linear combination of $M=50$ base planes) can generalize to highly diverse, complex, or unaligned real-world datasets (e.g., CO3D or OmniObject3D).

While the comparison with independent reconstruction baselines (like Instant-NGP, TensoRF, and K-Planes) is thorough, the paper lacks comparisons against other multi-scene meta-learning or auto-decoding baselines (e.g., standard latent-variable Tri-Plane models with a global decoder).

strengths: Clear motivation to address the computational bottleneck of scaling inverse graphics (NeRF reconstruction) to large datasets.
The proposed Micro-Macro decomposition of Tri-Planes is an intuitive way to split scene-specific and shared information, showing good efficiency gains in memory and optimization speed.
Extensive resource analysis (training time, memory) demonstrating significant savings compared to standard individual scene training.
Well-structured paper with clear algorithms, hyperparameters, and detailed experimental setups.
weaknesses: Weak baseline and misleading quality comparison: The paper compares against individual scene training of other NeRF representations. However, the quality (PSNR) of the proposed method (and its base Tri-Planes) is significantly lower than other standard methods. For example, in Table 4, TensoRF achieves 40.38 dB and Instant-NGP achieves 37.71 dB, while the proposed method only gets 31.20 dB (a massive drop of 6-9 dB). The claim 'without compromising rendering quality' is therefore highly misleading, as it only holds relative to a very weak Tri-Planes baseline.

Lack of comparison with proper scaling/few-shot/generalizable NeRF baselines: Scaling 3D reconstruction to large datasets is a well-studied problem. There are generalizable NeRFs, feed-forward models (like LRM, pixelNeRF), meta-learning-based initializations (Tancik et al., 2021), and autodecoder models (e.g., DeepSDF style, or Functa). The paper completely ignores comparisons against these paradigms, which are the standard ways to reconstruct scenes quickly and efficiently on large datasets.

Dataset simplicity and alignment assumptions: The method is evaluated only on highly simplified, clean, and centrally-aligned synthetic datasets (ShapeNet Cars and Basel Faces) at a low resolution (128x128). It is unclear how well the shared Macro-Planes and the 3D-aware latent space would generalize to complex, unaligned, or real-world datasets (e.g., outdoor scenes).

Dependency on a large pre-training set (N1=500): The first stage requires training on 500 scenes for over 31 hours. If the overall number of scenes is small, this overhead is not justified. This makes the method impractical for scenarios where a large, clean, domain-specific dataset is not available beforehand.
Minor typo: Figure 4 caption mentions 'ShapeNet Cats' instead of 'ShapeNet Cars'.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and practical problem: multi-scene inverse graphics (MSIG), which is a key bottleneck for training 3D generative models.
Proposes a novel and elegant Micro-Macro decomposition for planar representations (Tri-Planes), successfully separating scene-specific features from shared global structures.

Achieves impressive efficiency gains over standard Tri-Planes, with an approximate 7x speedup in per-scene training time and a 3x reduction in memory footprint, while actually improving the quality of Novel View Synthesis.
Provides a thorough evaluation against a diverse range of single-scene and multi-scene baselines, complemented by detailed per-scene results and full hyperparameter disclosure in the appendix.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to synthetic datasets (ShapeNet, Basel Faces) at a low resolution of 128x128. It remains unclear how well the shared 'macro' base planes generalize to complex, real-world scenes with cluttered backgrounds.

The training pipeline relies heavily on 'Anonymous (2025)' for the universal 3D-aware latent space and 3D regularization losses. This heavy dependency on an unpublished/anonymous reference slightly obscures the technical contribution of that specific component.

The two-stage training setup requires a large, diverse first subset of scenes ($S_1 = 500$) to bootstrap the shared base planes. The paper lacks an analysis of how the size or diversity of $S_1$ affects the generalization performance on the subsequent subset $S_2$.

While the planar structure is desirable for downstream 2D generative models, non-planar methods like SPARF-128 still outperform the proposed method in both reconstruction quality (PSNR) and per-scene training speed (0.82 min vs 8.92 min). A more balanced discussion on these trade-offs would strengthen the work.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and important problem: the high computational and memory cost of learning representations for large collections of 3D scenes (multi-scene inverse graphics).

The proposed Fused-Planes representation cleverly combines a scene-specific 'micro' component with a globally shared, dictionary-like 'macro' component. This decomposition, paired with training in a 3D-aware latent space, significantly compresses the scene representation.
The evaluation is thorough, comparing against a wide range of baselines (such as Tri-Planes, K-Planes, SPARF, and CodeNeRF) on ShapeNet and Basel Faces datasets.

The paper achieves an excellent trade-off between rendering quality, training speed, and storage footprint. The Fused-Planes-ULW variant, in particular, achieves an extremely low per-scene memory footprint (0.0008 MB) which is highly beneficial for storing large 3D datasets.
The submission is of high quality, providing clear explanations, a detailed training algorithm, thorough ablation studies, and comprehensive qualitative visualizations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The individual technical components have limited standalone novelty. The 3D-aware latent space is adopted from contemporary work (referred to as Anonymous, 2025), and representing scenes using a shared dictionary and coefficient combination is a classic concept in matrix/tensor decomposition.

The two-stage training scheme requires a relatively large and representative first subset of scenes ($N_1 = 500$) to learn the shared base planes and the latent space. This might limit its utility in scenarios where a diverse initial set is not available, or when learning out-of-distribution (OOD) scenes.

The experiments are conducted at a relatively low resolution of 128x128 pixels. It is not fully clear how the rendering quality, training speedups, and compression ratios scale to higher resolutions (e.g., 512x512 or higher) commonly used in modern 3D generation pipelines.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: the high resource consumption (training time and memory footprint) of learning representations for large collections of 3D scenes (multi-scene inverse graphics).
Introduces an intuitive decomposition of planar representations into scene-specific 'micro' planes and shared 'macro' base planes to improve efficiency.
Provides a comprehensive set of baselines, comparing against both single-scene methods (e.g., Instant-NGP, 3DGS, K-Planes) and multi-scene methods (e.g., CodeNeRF, SPARF, Tri-Planes).
Successfully reduces the memory footprint and training time compared to the standard Tri-Planes baseline while achieving better novel view synthesis quality (+2.3 dB PSNR improvement on ShapeNet).
weaknesses: Extremely limited evaluation set: The quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) in Table 1 are averaged over only 4 randomly sampled scenes per category (16 scenes for ShapeNet, 4 for Basel Faces). Evaluating on such a small number of scenes introduces high statistical variance and makes the quantitative claims unreliable.

Over-reliance on unreleased or concurrent work: The paper relies heavily on 'Anonymous (2025)' for its core technical components, including the universal 3D-aware latent space, the 3D regularization losses, and the latent NeRF training pipeline. Because this reference is anonymous and not fully detailed in a self-contained manner, it is impossible to properly verify, reproduce, or assess the technical soundness of the proposed method.

Lack of downstream task evaluation: The primary motivation for preserving the planar (Tri-Plane) structure over non-planar representations is 'interoperability with image models' (such as 2D CNNs and diffusion models). However, the paper does not showcase any downstream application (e.g., 3D generation, text-to-3D, or feed-forward reconstruction) using the trained Fused-Planes to validate this core motivation.

Performance trade-off: Fused-Planes still exhibits a massive performance gap compared to single-scene representations (e.g., 30.47 dB PSNR vs. 36.74 dB for TensoRF on ShapeNet). Moreover, the non-planar multi-scene baseline SPARF-128 outperforms Fused-Planes in both quality (31.07 dB vs. 30.47 dB PSNR) and training speed (0.82 min vs. 8.96 min per scene), undermining the practical utility of the proposed method unless the planar format is proven necessary via downstream tasks.
